title: Distributional Semantics & the Vector-Space View
oneLineScope: Meaning from co-occurrence — the vector-space view of words, from Firth and Harris.
prose:
You have been here before. Zellig Harris laid it out in 1954: morphemes and words with similar distributions — that is, appearing in similar sets of surrounding contexts — tend to be semantically related. John Rupert Firth sharpened it into its most quoted form three years later: “You shall know a word by the company it keeps.” This is the distributional hypothesis, and for the next sixty years it was the primary computational theory of how meaning could be extracted from text without explicit annotation. What the neural era did was not abandon this idea but accelerate and deepen it. Understanding where distributional semantics ends and where word2vec begins is the cleanest way to see what the neural turn actually added.

From co-occurrence to vectors

The first concrete realization of the hypothesis is the term–context matrix. Fix a vocabulary of \(V\) words (the rows) and a set of context tokens or context windows (the columns). For each word \(w_i\) and context \(c_j\), enter a count: how many times does \(w_i\) appear in a window that contains \(c_j\)? The result is a matrix \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times V}\) (or \(V \times D\) if you define \(D\) distinct context types). Each row is now the word’s co-occurrence profile — a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^V\) that records how that word distributes itself across contexts. Words with similar distributions get similar row vectors, and cosine similarity between those rows becomes an operational measure of semantic relatedness. No parser, no lexicon, no annotator: semantics as geometry, extracted from raw co-occurrence.

This is not a metaphor. If bank appears near deposit, loan, and interest in some documents, and near river, erodes, and current in others, its row vector will sit between the finance cluster and the nature cluster in the resulting space. The ambiguity is encoded structurally, not resolved — a point we will return to.

Raw counts, PPMI, and the weighting problem

Raw counts are a poor choice as cell entries: very frequent words like the and of co-occur with almost everything, dominating every row and washing out genuine semantic signal. The standard remedy is Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI), defined as:

\[ \text{PMI}(w, c) = \log_2 \frac{p(w, c)}{p(w)\,p(c)} \]

where \(p(w, c)\) is the joint probability (proportion of \((w, c)\) co-occurrence pairs in the corpus), and \(p(w)\), \(p(c)\) are the marginals. A high PMI means the word and context appear together more often than their individual frequencies would predict — a clean information-theoretic notion of specificity. The practical variant is PPMI (Positive PMI), which floors negative values at zero, since negative associations are unreliable in sparse matrices. The resulting PPMI matrix is sparser and far more discriminating than raw counts.

Dimensionality reduction: LSA as truncated SVD

Even with PPMI weighting, the raw co-occurrence matrix is enormous (\(V \times V\) with \(V\) easily in the hundreds of thousands), extremely sparse, and noisy. The natural next step — and one you will recognize immediately from factor analysis — is low-rank approximation by Singular Value Decomposition. Apply the truncated SVD to \(M\):

\[ M \approx U_k \Sigma_k V_k^{\top} \]

where \(U_k \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times k}\), \(\Sigma_k \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) (diagonal, non-negative), and \(V_k \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times k}\) are the rank-\(k\) factors, with \(k \ll V\) (typically 100–300). The rows of \(U_k \Sigma_k\) become the dense, low-dimensional word representations. This is precisely Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), introduced by Deerwester et al. in 1990 for information retrieval.

From a factor-analytic perspective, LSA discovers the latent dimensions of meaning that best reconstruct the observed co-occurrence patterns, analogous to principal components of the PPMI matrix. The compression does two things simultaneously: it reduces noise (rare, idiosyncratic co-occurrences are absorbed by the discarded small singular values) and it induces generalization (words that share many context neighbors will end up nearby even if they never co-occurred directly). Synonymy and near-synonymy become geometrically local. Harris’s distributional equivalence relation, which he had stated as a linguistic principle, turns out to be captured by the dominant singular structure of the co-occurrence matrix.

The limits of counting

Count-based distributional semantics works, but it carries three persistent liabilities.

First, sparsity: most \((w, c)\) pairs never appear in any finite corpus, so most matrix entries are zero. PPMI helps at the edges, but the core problem remains — rare words have unreliable profiles.

Second, static conflation: each word type gets one vector, regardless of context. Bank in “river bank” and bank in “central bank” are forced to share the same representation, which is the weighted average of all their contexts. Polysemy is smeared, not modeled. (This is not a failure of the hypothesis; it is a failure of the one-vector-per-type commitment.)

Third, scale and cost: assembling, weighting, and factorizing a \(V \times V\) PPMI matrix is expensive when \(V\) is large, and each dimension of the resulting vectors is still interpretable only in aggregate. The representations are distributed over many dimensions but in a particular way that is hard to learn from, or use in, downstream gradient-based systems.

The bridge forward

The neural approach does not throw out the distributional hypothesis — it doubles down on it. Word2vec and GloVe, covered in the next node, still learn from co-occurrence; they simply replace the count-then-factorize pipeline with a prediction objective trained by gradient descent. The resulting dense vectors (embeddings) of dimension \(d\) — typically 100–300 — are not explicitly the SVD factors of any matrix, but Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed that the skip-gram objective with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix, closing the theoretical loop back to Harris and Firth.

The second shift is deeper: transformer-era models make representations contextual. Rather than committing to one vector per word type, a transformer computes a different representation for each token occurrence, conditioned on the full surrounding context. Attention, at its mathematical core, is the mechanism that does that conditioning — a differentiable, content-addressed lookup that finally lets the system distinguish bank the institution from bank the landform at inference time. The Firth intuition survives intact; what changes is the granularity at which it is applied.

Three context windows radiate outward, each showing a short token sequence with bank highlighted: context A shows river bank erodes with neighbors river and erodes labeled in green; context B shows deposit bank teller with neighbors deposit and teller labeled in blue; context C shows bank lends money with neighbors lends and money labeled in blue. Arrows from each context point to the center. A box on the right labeled distributional signature of bank accumulates the neighbors from all contexts, with a note that the co-occurrence vector captures both senses and that static vectors conflate them.

bibliography.citation: Harris, Z. S. (1954). Distributional Structure. Word, 10(2–3), 146–162.
bibliography.annotation: The founding paper. Harris states the distributional hypothesis as a linguistic principle and defines it operationally in terms of substitutability in contexts. Read this for the intellectual origin of the entire vector-space approach to semantics; the argument is linguistic, not computational, but it is the bedrock everything else rests on.

bibliography.citation: Deerwester, S., Dumais, S. T., Furnas, G. W., Landauer, T. K., & Harshman, R. (1990). Indexing by Latent Semantic Analysis. Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 41(6), 391–407.
bibliography.annotation: The LSA paper. Introduces truncated SVD of a term–document matrix as a way to extract latent semantic structure for information retrieval. §2–3 cover the matrix construction and SVD; §4 gives the retrieval experiments. The place to go for the mathematical details of the count-then-factorize approach.

bibliography.citation: Firth, J. R. (1957). A synopsis of linguistic theory 1930–1955. In Studies in Linguistic Analysis (pp. 1–32). Blackwell.
bibliography.annotation: The source of the famous dictum. The broader essay is a statement of Firth's contextual theory of meaning; the distributional hypothesis is one instantiation of it. Worth reading for the original framing, which is more nuanced than the soundbite suggests.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed., draft), Chapter 6: Vector Semantics and Embeddings.
bibliography.annotation: The best practitioner-level treatment of the path from co-occurrence matrices through PPMI and LSA to word2vec. §6.1–6.5 cover the count-based foundations; §6.6–6.8 the transition to neural embeddings. The notation is clean and the worked examples are useful. The chapter to read alongside both this node and the word-embeddings node.
